title: How a Plane Toilet Flushes at 35,000 Feet ✈️
description:
How does an airplane toilet flush? Plane toilets are vacuum toilets: a valve opens the bowl to the thin air outside, the higher cabin pressure shoves everything into a tank at the back, and below 16,000 feet an electric vacuum pump does the job instead.

Sources:
https://satelliteindustries.com/blog/vacuum-toilet-system-in-aircraft
https://thepointsguy.com/news/how-airplane-toilets-work/
https://aerocorner.com/blog/how-airplane-toilets-work/

Animated in the Synthwave Outrun style.

topic: How does a plane toilet flush at 35,000 feet?
script:
How does a plane toilet flush
at thirty-five thousand feet?
It barely uses water.
It uses the sky.
Your cabin is pressurized,
packed with air like a balloon.
Outside, the air is super thin.
Press the button,
and a valve opens a pipe
from the bowl to that thin outside air.
The high pressure in the cabin
shoves everything down the pipe.
That's the whoosh.
It all lands in a tank at the back of the plane.
About three seconds later,
the valve slams shut.
But below sixteen thousand feet,
the outside air isn't thin enough,
so an electric pump makes the vacuum instead.
And no, nothing gets dumped in the sky.
Ground crews empty the tank after landing.
So, next flight,
are you brave enough to press it?
key_facts: Airplane toilets are vacuum toilets (patented by James Kemper in 1975, on Boeing jets by 1982)
At altitude a valve connects the bowl to low outside pressure; higher cabin pressure pushes waste through
Waste goes to a tank at the rear of the aircraft
Below about 16,000 ft (and on the ground) an electric vacuum generator creates the suction
Waste is not dumped in flight; ground service trucks empty the tank after landing
